strengths: Compelling adaptation of Native Sparse Attention (NSA) to multimodal video understanding: VideoNSA introduces a modality-aware hybrid scheme where vision tokens leverage hardware-aware sparse attention while text retains dense grouped-query attention, preserving textual instruction-following while scaling video context up to 128K tokens.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The method is validated across diverse benchmarks spanning long-video understanding (LongVideoBench, MLVU, TimeScope, LongTimeScope), visual temporal reasoning (Tomato), and spatial understanding (VSIBench), consistently outperforming both training-free token compression and training-free sparse attention baselines.

Extensive and insightful empirical findings: The paper presents six well-investigated findings covering context length scaling beyond training limits, attention budget allocation between global selection and local sliding window, gating evolution across network depth, latency/computational bottlenecks, and attention sink dynamics across branches.

Thorough ablation studies and transparency: The manuscript provides extensive ablations on branch selection, static vs. dynamic routing, transfer of sparse-trained weights to dense inference, and honestly characterizes engineering bottlenecks such as Triton query-head padding overheads.
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The core attention formulation directly adopts the tripartite branch design (compression, top-k selection, and sliding window) of Native Sparse Attention (NSA, Yuan et al., 2025c); the main conceptual contribution lies in its application, tuning, and analysis in the video-language domain rather than a fundamentally new operator.

High compute requirements: Unlike training-free sparse attention or token-pruning methods, VideoNSA requires end-to-end fine-tuning consuming ~4,600 H100 GPU hours, which limits accessibility and rapid prototyping across different backbones.

Kernel and hardware implementation gaps: Due to the head configuration of Qwen2.5-VL (28 query heads padded to 64 to meet Triton kernel alignment constraints), practical inference wall-clock speedups lag behind theoretical FLOP reductions, achieving moderate speedups over full attention compared to some training-free alternatives at shorter contexts.

Minor presentation issues: The title page contains empty placeholder fields ('Project page:', 'Code:', 'Model:'), and minor typos exist in the supplementary text (e.g., 'Tavke 15' on page 23, 'Iiterature' on page 19).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across a wide range of long video understanding, fine-grained temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding benchmarks (e.g., LongVideoBench, MLVU, TimeScope, LongTimeScope, Tomato, and VSIBench).

Principled adaptation of Native Sparse Attention (NSA) to multimodal LLMs by designing a modality-aware hybrid scheme (dense GQA for text, frame-aligned sparse branches for video) that retains instruction-following while scaling visual sequence lengths.

Extensive and insightful analysis of scaling behaviors, including the trade-off between temporal density and spatial resolution under fixed budgets, attention allocation between global and local windows, and routing-path dynamics.

In-depth investigation of attention sink behavior and layer-wise gating dynamics, showing how dynamic gating counteracts compression-induced sinks and how gating patterns specialize across network depth.
weaknesses: The core sparse attention formulation is adapted directly from NSA (Yuan et al., 2025c); while the multimodal hybrid adaptation and frame-block mapping are practical and effective, the algorithmic novelty of the underlying attention mechanism itself is somewhat incremental.

Real-world speedups on modern GPU hardware are constrained by implementation overheads (e.g., Triton kernel head padding for 28 query heads to 64), causing practical latency gains to fall short of theoretical FLOP reductions and trail some training-free sparse baselines (like XAttention and MInference at moderate context lengths).

Performance improvements over the original Qwen2.5-VL baseline on several standard benchmarks (e.g., MLVU and LongVideoBench) are relatively modest given the significant training cost (4,600 H100 GPU hours).

strengths: Timely and relevant exploration of adapting learnable, hardware-aware native sparse attention (NSA) to multimodal video-language models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) to tackle ultra-long video contexts.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across a wide suite of long-video, temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding benchmarks (e.g., LongVideoBench, LongTimeScope, TimeScope, MLVU, Tomato, VSIBench).

Detailed analysis and ablation studies providing insights into routing-gate dynamics across layers, inter-head correlations, the trade-off between temporal frame density vs. spatial tokens per frame, and the mitigation of attention sinks.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: The core sparse attention framework (combining token compression, top-k block selection, and sliding window with dynamic gating) is directly adopted from text-domain Native Sparse Attention (NSA), with standard grouped-query attention retained for text tokens.

Questionable baseline behavior during supervised fine-tuning: In Table 1 and Table 3, fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL with dense attention (Dense-SFT) causes performance drops across several benchmarks compared to the zero-shot base model (e.g., TimeScope drops from 81.0 to 76.8, LongVideoBench from 58.7 to 57.8). While the authors attribute this to training data quality, it confounds whether VideoNSA's gains stem from superior modeling capacity or from sparsity acting as a regularizer against suboptimal fine-tuning data.

Practical inference latency limitations: Due to implementation constraints (such as padding query heads from 28 to 64 to fit Triton kernel requirements) and memory-access bottlenecks in the compression branch, VideoNSA exhibits significant overhead. As shown in Figure 26b, it is substantially slower than Flash Attention at sequence lengths under 32K (achieving only 0.2x–0.5x relative speed) and lags behind training-free sparse baselines like XAttention across most context regimes.

Incomplete drafting and presentation issues: The paper contains placeholder artifacts on the title page ('Project page:', 'Code:', 'Model:' are left blank), noticeable typos and formatting errors (e.g., 'Tavke 15' on page 23, 'VideoNSAachieves' on page 22, and grammar inconsistencies), which detract from the overall quality of the submission.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical analysis investigating the interplay between temporal frame sampling, spatial token budgets (TPF), and sparse attention configurations up to 128K context length.
Interesting mechanistic observations regarding layer-wise gating dynamics, inter-head gate correlations, and the emergence/suppression of attention sinks across the three sparse branches.
Substantial engineering effort involved in integrating and training a hardware-aware native sparse attention mechanism on a 7B multimodal backbone using a large-scale video dataset.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The core attention mechanism is directly adopted from Native Sparse Attention (NSA, Yuan et al., 2025b). The adaptation to video consists primarily of treating one frame as one block and applying average pooling, while keeping text tokens dense, which represents an incremental architectural contribution.

High compute cost with marginal empirical gains: Adapting VideoNSA required 4,600 H100 GPU hours of end-to-end fine-tuning. Despite this heavy training budget, its performance is often nearly indistinguishable from or only marginally better than completely training-free sparse attention methods (e.g., MInference achieves 44.4 on LTS and 36.6 on VSIBench vs. VideoNSA's 44.4 and 36.0; on TimeScope VideoNSA gets 83.7 vs. XAttention's 83.1).

Degradation from the fine-tuning baseline: The fine-tuned dense model (`Flash Attn + SFT`) performs worse than the out-of-the-box base model (`Flash Attn`) across several benchmarks (e.g., drops from 58.7 to 57.8 on LVB, and 81.0 to 76.8 on TimeScope). This suggests potential issues or domain collapse in the 216K training subset/recipe, which complicates interpreting how much gain stems from the sparse architecture versus the training data.

Lack of complete end-to-end system benchmarking: While Figure 6 analyzes the latency per branch, the paper lacks realistic end-to-end wall-clock latency, throughput (tokens/sec or FPS), and peak VRAM reduction benchmarks comparing VideoNSA to FlashAttention-2 and competitive training-free methods during both prefill and generation stages.

Noticable presentation errors and lack of rigor in the appendix: Table 27 is titled as evaluating MLVU across attention budget strategies, but the table headers and scores are an exact duplicate copy-paste of the Tomato benchmark from Table 28. There are also several typographical errors throughout the draft (e.g., 'capbility', 'imrpove', 'Tavke 13', 'meterial').

strengths: Practical and timely adaptation of Native Sparse Attention (NSA) to multimodal video understanding, pairing dense attention for text tokens with hardware-aware NSA for vision tokens.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple diverse benchmarks including long-form video understanding (LongVideoBench, MLVU, TimeScope, LongTimeScope), visual temporal reasoning (Tomato), and spatial reasoning (VSIBench), consistently outperforming training-free token compression and sparse attention baselines.

Extensive analysis and diagnostic studies: provides insightful findings regarding information budget allocation (temporal frame rate vs. spatial token density), attention budget allocation (global blocks vs. local sliding window), inter-head gate correlation across layers, and the impact of sparsity on dynamic attention sinks.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is relatively limited: the core three-branch sparse attention framework is directly taken from NSA (Yuan et al., 2025b), and keeping text dense while sparsifying visual tokens is an intuitive and existing practice in multimodal efficiency literature.

Lack of complete end-to-end system speedup comparisons: while Figure 6 profiles the inference latency of individual attention branches, the paper lacks concrete end-to-end generation latency, time-to-first-token (TTFT), and GPU memory reduction figures compared against dense FlashAttention and training-free sparse baselines on full benchmarks.

Baseline comparability and training data impact: VideoNSA requires substantial computational resources (4600 H100 GPU hours) to fine-tune ViT + MLP + LLM, whereas many compared sparse attention methods are training-free. Furthermore, Dense-SFT exhibits performance drops compared to the base model, leaving open questions about the quality/impact of the SFT dataset.

Presentation and formatting errors in the appendix: Table 27 (labeled as MLVU results) appears to be an exact copy-paste duplicate of Table 28 (Tomato results), including identical subtask column headers and numerical values. In addition, several ablation rows in Tables 24, 25, and 29 display 0.0 across all metrics without explanation.

strengths: Relevant and timely problem: Addressing the quadratic computational bottleneck of long-context video understanding without suffering from the irreversible information loss common to token compression methods.

First integration of natively trainable sparse attention (NSA) into video-language models, scaling context up to 128K tokens and demonstrating that sparse connectivity can be learned end-to-end for spatio-temporal video data.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across a diverse suite of benchmarks covering long-form video understanding (LongVideoBench, MLVU, TimeScope, LongTimeScope), fine-grained temporal reasoning (Tomato), and spatial reasoning (VSIBench).

Detailed analysis and diagnostic insights, including the exploration of information allocation trade-offs (temporal sampling vs. spatial resolution), gating behavior across network depth, latency profiling across branches, and a study of attention sink emergence and suppression under sparse attention.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: The core attention mechanism (combining compression, top-k selection, and sliding window with dynamic gating) is directly adopted from Native Sparse Attention (NSA, Yuan et al., 2025b). The primary contribution lies in applying NSA specifically to visual tokens while keeping dense/GQA attention for text tokens in Qwen2.5-VL.

Modest performance improvements over training-free baselines: VideoNSA requires substantial computational resources to train (4,600 H100 GPU hours), yet its performance gains over training-free sparse attention methods (e.g., MInference and XAttention) are marginal. On VSIBench, training-free methods slightly outperform VideoNSA (36.5/36.6 vs. 36.1), and on LongTimeScope, MInference matches VideoNSA (44.4).

Negative impact of supervised fine-tuning data: The dense fine-tuned baseline (Dense-SFT / Flash Attn + SFT) consistently underperforms the original pre-trained Qwen2.5-VL-7B across multiple benchmarks (e.g., 57.8 vs. 58.7 on LongVideoBench, 76.8 vs. 81.0 on TimeScope), which complicates the interpretation of how much benefit stems from sparse attention versus artifacts of the 216K training set.

Missing end-to-end wall-clock speedup and throughput comparisons: While Figure 6 breaks down inference latency among the three sparse branches, the paper lacks end-to-end runtime, memory footprint, and decoding/prefilling throughput comparisons against dense FlashAttention-2 or training-free sparse baselines at equivalent sequence lengths.

Presentation and formatting errors in the appendix: Table 27 is an exact duplicate of Table 28 (including task columns corresponding to Tomato rather than MLVU subtasks). Furthermore, several entries in Tables 24 and 29 report 0.0 scores across all metrics without explanation (e.g., whether these represent out-of-memory errors or unsupported configurations).
